source.title: Compute-Optimal Quantization-Aware Training
source.authors: A. Dremov; D. Grangier; Angelos Katharopoulos; Awni Y. Hannun

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or garbling; the supplied text includes the main paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests loss-scaling and compute-allocation behavior in the distinct setting of a full-precision-to-QAT training pipeline, rather than reproducing the original language-model pretraining experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports QAT-specific validation-loss scaling and optimal QAT-to-FP allocation. It does not directly test the original claim's standard held-out pretraining loss laws or the parameters-versus-tokens compute-optimal split. The QAT-allocation results are recorded as related but not covered by a version. Results cited from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Chinchilla-like loss law, with power-law terms in N and D plus QAT penalty terms, to 757 QAT runs and 374 full-precision runs (86M–759M). This bears on whether the power-law form carries over to the FP→QAT training regime (V5). Its fitting-sensitivity results bear on V7. It does not test the parameter/token compute-optimal split, extrapolation of loss, architecture shape, or downstream tasks.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Correction: the 2.2B check validates the optimal QAT fraction predicted from the loss law, not loss prediction. The authors also propose QAT & learning-rate cooldown fusion, which gives consistent gains at 4–6 bits but mixed results at 1–2 bits. They also use the law to pick the optimal bit width under memory constraints.
record.recipe_differences: Studies a full-precision-to-QAT pipeline, fitting a QAT-specific loss law and optimizing the QAT-versus-FP token split; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token pretraining-loss measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The QAT loss fit is reported as highly dependent on initialization; MSE gives worse generalization than Huber loss. The alternate-dataset experiment changes dataset and pretraining/QAT batch sizes and learning rates; the DCLM-derived optimal-fraction fit has 0.111 MAE there.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal QAT fraction grows with tokens-per-parameter-byte (direct-fit MAE 0.091). The DCLM-derived fit transfers to SlimPajama with MAE 0.111.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss-optimal share of QAT relative to FP training increases with total tokens-per-parameter-byte and is predictable across sizes, bit widths and datasets.

record.problems: The authors state that the work focuses on a specific LLM architecture and exact results may differ across model types. The optimal-fraction fit is limited by the tested fraction grid and does not use all non-optimal points. The paper reports high fit sensitivity to initialization and notes poorer optimal-fraction prediction at low token counts. Most fit metrics are reported without uncertainty intervals.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many QAT fraction/token configurations and QAT cooldown-fusion comparisons, but these do not measure the standard pretraining loss laws or parameter-versus-token compute-optimal split in the claim. The separate 2.2B experiments test predicted QAT fractions and perplexities, not loss prediction from small-run power-law fits.

untested.parts: Standard pretraining loss power laws. The FP-only fit (B=16, R²=0.989) is embedded in the QAT formula with an interaction term and is not reported as a separate power law.
Loss extrapolation to much larger runs. The 2.2B check (2.9× larger) tests only the predicted optimal QAT fraction.
Effects of depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Disagreement between the Kaplan and Hoffmann laws; curvature away from a single power law in standard pretraining.

missing.what: Unified vs per-bit-width fits give very different exponents at similar R². The D exponent is 0.076 unified vs 0.38–0.72 per-bit; the N exponent is 0.21 unified vs 0.29–0.44 per-bit. This is direct evidence of fitting-choice dependence of exponents.
missing.locator: Appendix D Figure 8; Appendix G Figure 11, Table 5

missing.what: On SlimPajama, the optimal fraction inferred from the loss law has MAE 0.129, vs 0.111 for the direct fraction fit. The authors expect the loss-law fit to depend on data quality.
The full-precision loss fit (B=16 within the unified law) reaches R²=0.989, MAE=0.022 over 374 FP checkpoints.
Bootstrap parameter-significance tests: all terms except the constant shifts are significant.

record.verdict_notes: The record's peer_reviewed field (ICLR 2025) looks doubtful: the text is arXiv v2 dated Feb 2026 and gives no venue. Chen et al.'s QAT law, which the authors criticise for diverging as D grows, is a cited result and not a row. The V5 support depends on reading QAT as a distinct 'training regime'.

versions.untested_parts: Standard held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.

Prediction of loss for runs orders of magnitude larger from power laws fitted on smaller runs. The paper tests prediction of an optimal QAT fraction for a larger model, not this loss-prediction claim.
The loss-minimising parameter-count and token-count split under a fixed training compute budget. The paper studies the QAT-versus-FP token allocation instead.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and training regimes besides the tested text-model QAT pipeline; the paper uses a specific LLM architecture and QAT setup.
Downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Whether the published Kaplan and Hoffmann laws disagree, and whether their standard pretraining-loss curves bend away from a single power law.
